title: Does a heavier pendulum swing slower?
hook: Swap a 100 g weight for 2 kg on the same string. Does the beat change?

knows: what a pendulum and a swing are
doesNotKnow: Newton's second law in equation form
the formula T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g)

misconception: A heavier bob swings more slowly (or faster) because it has more weight; the mass sets the rhythm.
objective: The learner can explain that a pendulum's period depends on its length, not its mass, because extra weight pulls harder but is exactly that much harder to accelerate; and that four times the length doubles the period.

claims.text: For an ideal pendulum (point mass on a light string, no air drag) the period does not depend on the mass of the bob.
claims.source: Equation of motion m L theta'' = -m g sin(theta): m cancels. Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 15 (The Simple Pendulum).

claims.text: For small swings the period is T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g); a 1 m pendulum on Earth (g = 9.81 m/s^2) has a period of about 2.0 s.
claims.source: Small-angle approximation sin(theta) ~ theta of c1's equation. Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 15. 2 pi sqrt(1 / 9.81) = 2.006 s.

claims.text: Making the string four times longer doubles the period.
claims.source: T is proportional to sqrt(L), from c2.

claims.text: The simulation integrates the full equation theta'' = -(g / L) sin(theta) from a 20 degree release; at that amplitude the period is about 0.8% longer than the small-angle formula.
claims.source: Exact period T = T0 * 2K(k)/pi with k = sin(10 deg); series T ~ T0 (1 + theta0^2/16 + 11 theta0^4/3072) = 1.0077 T0. Thornton and Marion, Classical Dynamics of Particles and Systems, sec. 4.4.

claims.text: Mass cancels because a heavier bob is pulled harder by gravity in exact proportion to how much harder it is to speed up.
claims.source: Gravitational force m g and inertia m appear on both sides of F = m a (equivalence of gravitational and inertial mass). Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 5 and 15.

claims.text: Galileo reported that pendulums of equal length swing in step whatever their weight.
claims.source: Galileo Galilei, Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences (1638), First Day, the experiment with lead and cork pendulums.

claims.text: Gravity pulls 20 times harder on a 2 kg bob than on a 100 g bob, and the 2 kg bob is also 20 times harder to speed up.
claims.source: Weight m g and inertia m both scale with mass; 2 kg / 0.1 kg = 20.

claims.text: With a 20 degree release, a 1 m pendulum has a period of 2.02 s and a 0.25 m pendulum about 1 s, so four times the length doubles the period; 1.75 m and 2.00 m strings give 2.67 s and 2.86 s.
claims.source: Exact period T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g) / AGM(1, cos(theta0 / 2)) with g = 9.81, theta0 = 20 deg: 2.0215 s (1 m), 1.0107 s (0.25 m), 2.6741 s (1.75 m), 2.8588 s (2 m). Ratio T(1) / T(0.25) = 2 exactly because the amplitude is the same.

claims.text: A playground swing that takes 3 seconds per back-and-forth with a child on it still takes about 3 seconds with an adult twice as heavy sitting on it the same way.
claims.source: Recall question. Treat the swing as a pendulum: the period depends on length, not mass (c1). Idealisation: rider and seat are not a point mass, so a real adult sitting differently shifts the effective length; 'the same way' is the stated condition.

recall.question: A playground swing takes 3 seconds per back-and-forth with a child on it. An adult twice as heavy sits on it the same way. About how long per swing now?
recall.why: The period depends on the length of the chain, not the weight: extra weight pulls harder but is equally harder to move.
